Atomicity: a transaction is all-or-nothing and is rolled back if any step fails. Consistency: it takes the database from one valid state to another without violating constraints. Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's uncommitted changes. Durability: once committed the data survives crashes, e.g. via write-ahead logging.
ACID stands for atomicity, consistency, isolation and durability. Atomicity means a transaction either fully happens or not at all.

Durability just means the database keeps recent data in memory so reads are always fast, and isolation means transactions are run strictly one after another on a single thread so two can never run at the same time. Consistency is about replicating data to every server.

Bubble sort walks along the list comparing each pair of neighbouring elements and swaps the pair when it is out of order, so the biggest values drift to the end. Its running time is O(n²) on average and in the worst case, and it is mainly taught as an introductory example.
Bubble sort splits the list in half recursively and merges the sorted halves, giving O(n log n) time.

Each pass swaps neighbouring elements that are out of order, which pushes the largest remaining element to the end. With n items that is up to n-1 passes of up to n-1 comparisons, so quadratic time; if you stop when a pass makes no swaps, already-sorted input costs only O(n).

A generator function uses yield, so calling it returns an iterator that produces values lazily and pauses at each yield, which keeps memory constant. For example: def fib(limit): a, b = 0, 1; while a < limit: yield a; a, b = b, a + b.
A generator function builds the whole list in memory and returns it with return, which makes it faster than a normal function.

Training-serving skew is a mismatch between how features are produced in training and in serving, for example cents offline and dollars online, or -1 versus 0 for missing values; the world has not changed. Data drift is the real-world input distribution changing over time while the pipelines stay consistent. To tell them apart, replay raw events through both feature paths and compare: differences on the same event mean skew; shifts only across time mean drift.
Training-serving skew and data drift are the same thing: the model just got old. You fix both by retraining every week.
Skew is when the features computed during training differ from those at serving, for instance different units.
